subject: Banking
title: How SWIFT Moves Trillions
description: A fast breakdown of How SWIFT Moves Trillions for builders.

hook.text: SWIFT handles $5 trillion in daily transfers across 200 countries. It is the backbone of global money movement.

buildup.text: SWIFT does not move money itself. It sends secure messages between banks telling them to credit or debit accounts.

discovery.text: A wire from New York to Tokyo passes through correspondent banks. Each bank in the chain takes a fee and adds delay.

twist.text: Sanctions enforcement relies on SWIFT. Cutting Russia from SWIFT in 2022 was a financial weapon, not a technical one.

climax.text: SWIFT is infrastructure and power. Controlling the messaging system means controlling access to global finance.

punchline.text: $5 trillion daily via messages. SWIFT is finance's nervous system.

quiz.question: What does SWIFT actually transmit?
options: Secure messages between banks instructing transfers

details.summary: SWIFT is a messaging network that connects over 11,000 financial institutions in 200 countries, transmitting standardized payment instructions that enable trillions of dollars in cross-border transfers daily.
details.whyItMatters: SWIFT does not actually move money but coordinates its movement globally. Its near-monopoly on international payment messaging makes it a powerful geopolitical tool, as Russia discovered when cut off in 2022.
takeaways: SWIFT transmits payment messages but does not hold or transfer funds
Over 11,000 institutions in 200 countries use the SWIFT network
Disconnection from SWIFT effectively isolates a country financially

faq.question: Why is SWIFT so powerful if it only sends messages?
faq.answer: SWIFT messages are the standardized language banks use to instruct each other to move money. Without SWIFT, banks cannot communicate payment instructions internationally in a trusted, standardized way, effectively cutting off cross-border finance.

faq.question: What happened when Russia was cut off from SWIFT?
faq.answer: Major Russian banks lost the ability to communicate with international banks, severely disrupting trade, remittances, and financial flows. Russia had to use workarounds and alternative systems, but at much higher cost and friction.
